rules.rule: When answering about personality change, separate stable core tendency from changing expression, self-development, or mean-level trend.
rules.reason: The professor repeatedly resists all-or-nothing answers and pushes students to specify the level of change they mean.

rules.rule: For socioemotional selectivity, open with limited-time perception rather than energy loss, frailty, or passive withdrawal.
rules.reason: The professor explicitly rejects decline-only explanations and reframes the theory around motivational change tied to time perception.

rules.rule: When explaining the SOC model, tie it to handling decline, loss, and reduced resources rather than saying older adults can simply do everything as before.
rules.reason: The lecture frames SOC as a strategy for successful aging under real constraint, not as empty optimism.

rules.rule: If you mention personality and health, connect the trait to repeated behavior over decades and then to the health outcome.
rules.reason: The professor accepts the personality-health link only when it is explained through accumulated behavior and not as a magical one-step effect.

rules.rule: For stage theories, say what each theorist adds and where the empirical limit lies, especially for Levinson.
rules.reason: The lecture praises insight but immediately asks about sample, cohort, and evidence strength.

rules.rule: Use the exact names and English terms when they matter: OCEAN, neuroticism, socioemotional selectivity theory, SOC, Erikson, Loevinger, Levinson, and Paul Baltes.
rules.reason: This session repeatedly turned on precise terminology, and fuzzy paraphrase would weaken oral answers immediately.

rules.rule: If you say a point was interesting or surprising, state what prior assumption changed and tie it back to the chapter immediately.
rules.reason: The stronger student moments in this class worked because they named the intuition they had first and then corrected it with the reading's logic.
